title: Reading a failed run
desc: Runs and log: the live strip, filters, step timeline, retry, and the snapshot that surprises people.
learningGoal: Go from 'it stopped working' to the exact step, the exact reason, and a green re-run.

steps.title: Nobody got the Monday report
steps.bodyMd:
Every Monday at 07:00 an automation at Van Dijk Groep builds the quote pipeline report and mails it to the sales lead. This Monday it did not arrive.

The answer lives in **Studio → Runs & log**: *"Every time an automation fired: what started it, what it did, and what went wrong."* It is the only Studio section about the past — you cannot create a run here, only read one.

It opens with three settings already applied: the scope on **My runs**, the range on **24h**, and the **Live or test** filter on **Live runs**. Remember those three. They are the reason people say "my run has disappeared".

steps.question: Anne tested that quote automation by hand last Tuesday, and today she cannot find the test run anywhere in Runs & log. Which two controls are hiding it?

choices.label: The Live or test filter, still on Live runs
The My runs / Organisation switch
choices.feedback: That switch decides whose runs you see, not which ones. Her own test run belongs in My runs, so switching to Organisation would not bring it back.

choices.label: The ninety-day clean-up of old runs
choices.feedback: Runs are kept for 90 days. A run from last Tuesday is nowhere near that line — it is the filters, not the clean-up.

steps.explanation: Two defaults hide it together: the range opens on 24h, and the Live or test filter opens on Live runs, which leaves test runs out. Widen the range to 7d or 30d and set Live or test to Live runs and tests (or Tests only). On a narrower screen that filter sits behind the Filter button. Mind what Clear does: it resets the trigger, Live or test and automation filters, but leaves the status chips and the range alone.

steps.title: One run, step by step
steps.bodyMd:
Anne clicks the **Failed** chip, widens the range to **7d**, and opens Monday's row. The run fills the screen.

The bar along the top carries the outcome, `took 4s`, what started it (`On a schedule`), a version chip like `v12`, and the reason in brackets.

Down the left is the **Steps** rail: one row per step with its status word, `· took …`, its own error line, and — only when a step ran more than once — `· attempt 2 of 2`. Click a step and a panel opens under the read-only canvas on the right: what that step was handed — **Input** — beside what it produced — **Output** — with the error in red above them.

That is the whole diagnosis: which step, what went in, what came out.

steps.title: "This is where it stopped"
steps.bodyMd:
Under the failing row the rail prints one sentence: **"This is where it stopped. Nothing ran after this point."** For Anne that matters more than the error itself — it means no half-finished mail went out to anyone.

Clicking the step also selects that node on the canvas, and the page's web address picks up the step, so a link you paste in chat opens on exactly that step — for the person who owns the run.

The reason is phrased twice on purpose. The **Now running** strip shows only the class — `failed — a connection is no longer signed in` — because the full message can quote a customer. The full text waits inside the run.

steps.title: From "it broke" to a green run
steps.instruction: Put Anne's five moves in the order that gets the Monday report out. Drag them into place.

items.label: In Runs & log, click the Failed chip and widen the range to 7d
Open the failed run of the quote automation
Follow the Steps rail to the red step and the line "This is where it stopped."
Press Open in editor and fix what that step needed
Come back to the run and press Run it again

sim.feedback: Narrow first, then read, then fix, then re-run. Fixing before you have found the red step is guessing, and re-running before the fix just produces a second identical failure — with the same reason, five minutes later.

steps.question: Anne reconnects the CRM in the editor, then reopens Monday's failed run. The canvas still shows the old step, exactly as it was. What is going on?

choices.label: A run always shows the saved version it actually ran — the v-chip in the bar — not today's automation
The page is cached; a refresh will show the fixed step
choices.feedback: It is not a caching problem. The run stores the definition as it was at the time, and renders that on purpose — a refresh changes nothing.

choices.label: Her fix was not saved
choices.feedback: Possible in general, but not what you are seeing here: even a saved fix leaves every earlier run showing the version that ran.

choices.label: Failed runs are frozen and cannot be re-read after a fix
choices.feedback: Failed runs stay fully readable for 90 days. What is frozen is the definition the run used, not your access to it.

steps.explanation: The timeline is a record, not a live view of the automation. It renders the version that ran, so the evidence still makes sense months later. Your fix shows up in the next run — which is why the bar's Run it again button is titled "Uses the automation as it is now".

steps.title: Two ways to try again
steps.bodyMd:
**The whole run.** In the run bar, **Run it again** starts a fresh run of the automation as it is now. It opens immediately, so you never hunt for it in the list, and its bar carries **"This was a retry of an earlier run"** — the link back to what you were fixing.

**One step.** In the editor, a failed step offers **Retry** — *"Retry this step and continue downstream from here"* — and an open step offers **Execute**, which runs that step alone on the data the earlier steps already produced. Faster, and it does not send the mail twice.

And nothing retries itself: a step tries again only if someone gave it a retry setting. Otherwise a failure stops the run right there — unless you wired that step's failure into its own **on error** path.

steps.question: Van Dijk's purchase-order automation pauses for approval, continues after Finance says yes, then pauses again on a second approval. How does Runs & log show that, and which run do the row's actions act on?

choices.label: One row for the whole journey, showing the newest leg's status — and the actions act on the leg that is actually live
One row per leg, each with its own actions
choices.feedback: Legs exist underneath, but the list deliberately collapses a journey into one row. Otherwise a three-page form would fill the log with rows nobody asked for.

choices.label: One row showing the status of the first leg, which started it all
choices.feedback: The opposite: the row shows the newest leg, because what you need to know is what it is doing now, not how it began.

choices.label: Nothing at all until the journey finishes
choices.feedback: A paused run is visible the whole time, with the outcome Waiting for approval — that is exactly when you most want to see it.

steps.explanation: An automation that pauses for an approval or a form resumes in a new leg. The list shows one row per journey with the newest leg's status, and the row's actions are aimed at the live leg, so Approve — and Stop it, which the row offers while a leg is still running — hit the run that is really there. Forms pause the same way, with the outcome Waiting for a form.

steps.title: Your turn: tell the person who was waiting
steps.instruction: Write the short message Anne sends the sales lead at Van Dijk Groep about the failed Monday report — three or four sentences, no jargon. A strong note names the automation and when it should have run, names the step it stopped at and the reason in plain words, says what did and did not happen afterwards, and ends with what you changed and what the re-run did. Keep customer data out of it: describe the reason, do not paste a step's input or output.
steps.placeholder: e.g. The Monday 07:00 quote pipeline report did not go out today. It stopped at the step that fetches the CRM data, because that connection was no longer signed in, and nothing after it ran — so no partial report was mailed to anyone. I have reconnected it and re-run the report; it finished at 09:12 with 14 quotes. Next Monday should be normal, and I will check it.

steps.title: Retry a failed run — we'll check it
steps.instruction: Open Studio → Runs & log, click the Failed chip and widen the range to 7d if the list looks empty. Open a failed run of your own, read the Steps rail down to the red step, fix what it needed, then press Run it again. No failure to hand? Make one on purpose: point a step in a test automation at something that does not exist, run it, then fix it and retry.

steps.title: Ninety days, and what your admin sees
steps.bodyMd:
Two limits to know before you lean on this screen.

**How long runs are kept.** Runs that have finished, failed or been stopped are removed after **90 days**. Runs that are still going or waiting for a person are never touched. If something has to be provable years later — who approved what — that record lives with the approval, not in the run log.

**The Organisation scope.** A colleague with an org-admin role can switch Runs & log to **Organisation** and see every automation's runs: the outcome, what happened, the error. They still cannot open someone else's run — every run page belongs to its owner — so those rows are not clickable. That view also does not refresh itself.

That is the loop: widen the filters until you find the run, follow the Steps rail to the red step, fix it in the editor, **Run it again**, and tell the person who was waiting what happened.

ex-automation-runs-failures-note.title: A failure note someone can act on
ex-automation-runs-failures-note.task: Write a three-or-four-sentence message to the colleague who was waiting for an automation's output, explaining a failed run: which automation and when, which step stopped it and why, what did and did not happen afterwards, and what was done about it.
criteria: Names the automation and the moment it should have delivered, and the step where it stopped.
Gives the reason in plain language a non-builder understands, rather than a raw error blob or a step id.
States the consequence — that nothing ran after the failing step, so the reader knows what did and did not go out.
Ends with the action taken: what was fixed and what the re-run did, or when it will be checked.
Keeps customer or colleague personal data out of the note; it describes the reason instead of quoting a step's data.
ex-automation-runs-failures-note.guidance: Do not pass a note that only says it failed and is being looked into, with no step and no reason. Do not pass a pasted stack trace or error dump with no sentence around it. Do not pass a note that quotes names, e-mail addresses or customer text lifted from a step's input or output. A note that honestly says the cause is not found yet still passes if it names the step, says nothing after it ran, and says when there will be news.

practiceTopic.title: Runs & log: finding and fixing a failed run
practiceTopic.summary: How the runs list filters, what a run's step timeline records, how to re-run, and what is kept.
facts: Studio → Runs & log opens on My runs, the 24h range and Live runs in the Live or test filter, so a test run or a run from last week is hidden until you widen the range or change that filter. Its status chips read All, Finished, Failed, Running, Waiting for someone and Stopped.
The Now running strip covers a fixed 24 hours, shows at most six automations with failures first, and prints the error class rather than the free-text message, which can quote a customer.
A run's step timeline renders the saved version of the automation that actually ran — shown as a version chip in the run bar — not today's definition.
After the failing step the Steps rail prints: This is where it stopped. Nothing ran after this point.
Run it again re-runs the automation as it is now; pressed from the run's own bar the new run opens immediately, and its bar carries the note that it was a retry of an earlier run.
Nothing retries itself: a step only tries again if it carries a retry setting, which is off by default; otherwise wire the step's failure into its own on error path.
Finished, failed and stopped runs are removed after 90 days; runs still going or waiting for a person are never removed.
The Organisation scope needs an org-admin role and shows outcome and error for everyone's runs, but those rows cannot be opened because every run page belongs to its owner.

actionChecks.label: Retry a failed run
actionChecks.hint: In Studio → Runs & log, open a failed run of your own and press Run it again.

endpoints.returns: { runs: [...] } — the caller's own runs; each row has id, status, startedAt, parentRunId, rootRunId

criteria.label: A run exists that was started as a retry
criteria.hint: Open a failed run and press Run it again — the retry opens straight away and its bar says it was a retry of an earlier run.
criteria.rule: at least one row in runs where parentRunId is not null and rootRunId equals that row's id
